faq.q: Why is CK higher in boys than girls?

faq.q: Can CK be normal in early rhabdomyolysis?

faq.a: Serial CK trends show muscle injury resolution; falling levels indicate effective management.

exam: A 7‑year‑old with severe malaria presents with dark urine – what is your immediate management and why? — Start aggressive IV fluids to prevent AKI; monitor electrolytes and CK; treat malaria promptly.

A child on propofol infusion for ventilation develops CK 8 000 U/L – what does this indicate and what steps do you take? — Suggests propofol infusion syndrome; stop propofol, give supportive fluids, check cardiac enzymes, consider alternative sedation.
How would you differentiate skeletal muscle injury from myocardial infarction using laboratory tests? — Compare CK iso‑enzymes (CK‑MM vs CK‑MB) and add troponin; ECG also helps.
A patient with hypothyroidism has CK 300 U/L – does this require urgent treatment? — No urgent action; treat underlying thyroid disease and re‑check CK after euthyroidism.

What are the key electrolyte abnormalities in rhabdomyolysis and their management? — Hyperkalaemia (treat with calcium gluconate, insulin/glucose), hypocalcaemia (usually correct after CK falls), hyperphosphataemia (monitor, dialysis if severe).

When is sodium bicarbonate indicated in rhabdomyolysis and why might it be unavailable? — Used to alkalinise urine when CK >5 000 U/L and dark urine persists; may be unavailable in low‑resource labs, then focus on fluids and close monitoring.

A child with suspected muscular dystrophy has persistently elevated CK but normal renal function – what long‑term plan do you advise? — Genetic testing, physiotherapy, cardiac surveillance, avoid nephrotoxins, educate family on trigger avoidance.
Why should NSAIDs be avoided in a child with rhabdomyolysis? — They can worsen renal perfusion and precipitate AKI.
ai.title: Creatine Kinase in Paediatrics
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Creatine kinase (CK) is an enzyme released from damaged muscle. In children it helps identify rhabdomyolysis, muscular dystrophies and drug‑induced injury, guiding urgent care and long‑term management.

b: Normal paediatric range: up to 190 U/L (varies with age and sex).
Three iso‑enzymes: CK‑MM (skeletal), CK‑MB (cardiac), CK‑BB (brain).
sections.p: CK is a cytosolic enzyme that catalyses the transfer of a phosphate group from ATP to creatine, providing rapid energy for muscle contraction. Serum CK rises when muscle cell membranes are disrupted.

b: Mild: CK 1‑5 × upper‑limit of normal (ULN).
Moderate: CK 5‑10 × ULN.
Severe: CK >10 × ULN or >5 000 U/L, high risk of AKI.
sections.p: Rhabdomyolysis severity is staged by peak CK level and presence of complications such as acute kidney injury (AKI).

b: Infections: severe malaria, dengue, HIV‑associated myopathy, bacterial sepsis.
Trauma: crush injury, prolonged immobilisation, burns.
Hereditary: Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy, limb‑girdle dystrophies.
Drugs/toxins: quinine, antiretrovirals (e.g., zidovudine), traditional herbal preparations.
Metabolic: hypothyroidism, electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia).
sections.p: In low‑resource African settings the most common precipitants are infections, trauma and hereditary muscle disease.

b: Myalgia or calf tenderness.
Pseudohyponatraemia from fluid shifts.
Tea‑coloured urine (myoglobinuria).
Reduced urine output if AKI develops.
sections.p: Children may present with muscle pain, swelling, dark urine, or be asymptomatic with only a lab abnormality discovered during work‑up for fever or trauma.

t.b: Is there muscle injury? – Elevated CK confirms myocyte damage; magnitude helps stage severity.
Is the source skeletal, cardiac or brain? – Predominant CK‑MM points to skeletal muscle; CK‑MB elevation suggests cardiac involvement.
Is myoglobinuria present? – Positive dipstick with few or no RBCs indicates myoglobin, supporting rhabdomyolysis.
Is there AKI? – Rising creatinine signals renal impairment; guide fluid therapy.
Are there life‑threatening shifts? – Hyperkalaemia or hypocalcaemia may need urgent correction.
Is hypothyroidism contributing? – Elevated TSH with high CK suggests myopathy of hypothyroidism.
Is there renal cortical echogenicity or obstruction? – Helps assess AKI cause when labs are limited.

b: CK >10 × ULN with rising creatinine – risk of AKI.
Severe hyperkalaemia (>6.0 mmol/L) – arrhythmia risk.
Persistent oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h) – urgent renal support needed.
Severe metabolic acidosis – may require bicarbonate.
sections.p: Prompt recognition prevents irreversible kidney damage and systemic complications.

b: Aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation (20 mL/kg bolus, then 1‑2 mL/kg/h) to maintain urine output >1 mL/kg/h.
Alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate only if urine remains dark and CK >5 000 U/L and bicarbonate is available.
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (e.g., NSAIDs, aminoglycosides).
Specific therapy: antimalarials for malaria, antibiotics for bacterial sepsis, thyroid hormone replacement for hypothyroidism, stop offending drug/herbal remedy.
Monitor CK, electrolytes and renal function every 6‑12 h until stable.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect the kidneys and correct electrolyte disturbances.

b: Repeat CK 1‑2 weeks after discharge to ensure decline.
Genetic counselling for dystrophies; physiotherapy to maintain function.
Vaccination and malaria prophylaxis to reduce infection‑related rhabdomyolysis.
Educate on safe use of traditional medicines.
sections.p: After acute recovery, assess for chronic muscle disease and educate families on avoidance of triggers.

b: Myocardial infarction – raises CK‑MB, not CK‑MM; ECG and troponin differentiate.
Hemolysis – may give positive urine dipstick for blood but no myoglobin; peripheral smear helps.
Severe dehydration – can raise CK modestly; history of muscle injury clarifies.
sections.p: Conditions that also cause elevated CK or similar symptoms.

b: Hemolysed serum can falsely elevate CK; repeat sample if haemolysis present.
CK may be normal early (<6 h) after injury; repeat if suspicion persists.
Hypothyroidism can cause modest CK rise; do not assume rhabdomyolysis without clinical signs.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly falling urine output, CK >10 × ULN, or hyperkalaemia >6.0 mmol/L – call senior clinician or arrange urgent transfer for dialysis.
